replenish

/rih-PLEN-ish/ — stress on PLEN · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To replenish something is to fill it back up again after it has been used or emptied.

Desert travelers plan each day's route around where they can replenish their water.

Worked Example

After the power outage, the hospital rushed to replenish the backup generators with diesel fuel before another storm hit the city.

Re (again) + Latin plenus (full) + -ish (to make) = to make full again. The generators were empty after running all night, so replenish precisely describes restoring them to full functional capacity. A simpler word like 'refuel' could work, but replenish conveys the urgency and purpose of restoring critical resources to readiness.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

supply: To supply is to provide whatever is needed, whether or not anything has run out — a spring supplies a village with water all year long. To replenish is specifically to fill a store back up after use has drained it. Supplying is ongoing provision; replenishing answers a shortage.

replace: To replace something is to swap it for a different one — a dead battery, a broken part goes out and a new one goes in. To replenish keeps the same store and fills it back up. You replace a worn tire; you replenish the pantry that a week of guests emptied.

stock up: To stock up is to gather extra of something before you need it, like buying canned food ahead of a storm. To replenish works after the fact: refilling a supply that has already been used or emptied. Stocking up prepares for a shortage; replenishing repairs one.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

deplete: use up until little remains

exhaust: use up completely, leaving nothing

Where it sits · how much of the supply is renewed — top off → refill → restock → replenish

top off vs. replenish: Topping off a glass adds just a splash, but replenishing the pantry means filling every empty shelf back up.

refill vs. replenish: You refill one water bottle at the fountain, while a desert outpost must replenish its entire water supply.

restock vs. replenish: A clerk restocks a single shelf of cereal, but replenishing the whole warehouse brings every supply back to full.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: again (Latin)

Root — plen

Root — plen: full (from plenus) (Latin)

Suffix — -ish

Suffix — -ish: verb-forming ending, as in finish and nourish (French)

Put it together

Put it together: Re- (again) + plen (full — think plenty) + -ish (a French verb ending) = 'to make full again': to fill a supply back up after it has been drained or used.

Use the root in a new word: plentiful

Use the root in a new word: plentiful: Thanks to the steady spring rains, the orchard's harvest was plentiful this year.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal-practical

Reach for replenish when describing the intentional restoration of something essential to its proper full level—it suggests both emptying and careful refilling. Common with supplies (water, fuel, oxygen), inventory (medical stock), and abstract resources (energy, resolve). It's more purposeful than 'refill' and implies preparation or recovery after depletion.
